options_ranked.title: Base Oil Cost Hedging and Supplier Renegotiation for Engine Oil Formulations
options_ranked.description: Run a 60-90 day procurement intervention on base oil supply contracts feeding Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil: (1) forward-curve hedging of index-linked base oil exposure, and (2) supplier renegotiation using volume commitments and longer-term fixed-price tranches to claw back 40-60% of the observed cost shock. Operates entirely on the COGS side, so it cannot breach the anchor-account price-lock. Scope: Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (Δ -7.14pp) is the primary target with spillover to Conventional; unaffected timeframe buckets and product lines within threshold need no action. A first-week measurement check confirms the decline is a real input-cost shock rather than a costing-allocation artifact before hedges are placed.
options_ranked.rationale: The synchronized, near-parity declines across Synthetic Blend (-7.14pp), Conventional (-6.61pp) and Compressor Oil (-5.86pp) are the signature of a shared input-cost mechanism, and base_oil_cost is a client-confirmed component of COGS, which directly moves Gross Margin %. Cost-side action is the only lever that is both grounded in confirmed causal edges and structurally immune to the price-lock constraint, making it the most defensible near-term recovery mechanism.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 60-90 days for renegotiated terms; hedging protects forward margin immediately upon execution

arguments_for: Directly targets the confirmed base_oil_cost-to-COGS mechanism behind the broadest pattern in the data — every major declining product shares this input.
Requires no customer-facing change, so it carries no volume or relationship risk and fully respects the price-lock constraint.
arguments_against: Hedging locks in current forward prices; if base oil prices fall, the business forgoes the downside benefit and the hedge becomes a cost.
Supplier renegotiation leverage depends on volume commitments the business may not want to make if the structural option later de-emphasizes Conventional.
key_questions: What proportion of base oil purchasing is currently index-linked and unhedged, and at what forward prices could 60-70% of volume be locked today?
Has the costing methodology (allocation, standard cost revisions) been ruled out as a contributor before treating the full 7.14pp as a real cost shock?

implementation_triggers: Measurement-integrity check confirms the margin decline is a genuine input-cost movement, not an overhead-allocation or standard-cost revision artifact.
Forward base oil curve offers lock-in prices below the trailing 90-day average paid.
prerequisites: Unit-cost bridge for Synthetic Blend (prior YTD vs current) decomposing base oil, distribution, manufacturing, and packaging contributions (Week 1).
Treasury approval of hedging mandate and counterparty limits.
Supplier spend concentration analysis identifying negotiation leverage points.

impact_estimate.basis: Base oil is a confirmed component of COGS; assuming base oil is 35-50% of COGS in blend formulations, hedging 60-70% of forward volume plus renegotiating supplier terms recovers 50-75% of the -7.14pp Synthetic Blend decline; this sizes the Synthetic Blend segment, with additional spillover on Conventional.

key_assumptions.assumption: The margin decline is predominantly a real base-oil input-cost shock rather than a costing-methodology artifact.
key_assumptions.provenance: Unit-cost bridge showing base oil cost per unit rose materially versus prior YTD would confirm; a flat input cost with revised overhead allocation would falsify.

key_assumptions.assumption: Base oil represents 35-50% of COGS in blend formulations, making procurement action material to the ratio.
key_assumptions.provenance: Bill-of-materials cost breakdown for Synthetic Blend; falsified if base oil is under 25% of COGS.

key_assumptions.assumption: Suppliers will concede price in exchange for volume or tenor commitments in the current market.
key_assumptions.provenance: Outcome of the first two supplier renegotiation rounds relative to a 3-5% unit-cost reduction target.

key_assumptions.assumption: COGS movements directly move Gross Margin % with revenue held constant.
key_assumptions.provenance: Client-confirmed causal edge: gross_margin_pct <-> cogs, with base_oil_cost a confirmed account_category component of COGS.

options_ranked.title: Tiered Contract Renegotiation and Mix Incentive Program for Post-Lockout Renewal Cycles
options_ranked.description: Identify anchor accounts whose Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil contracts expire after the current price-lock window, and prepare +3-5% renewal pricing on those SKUs. In parallel, launch a mix incentive (rebate or volume bonus) rewarding customers who shift allocation from Value-tier toward premium formulations during the lockout. Scope: the Engine Oils line (Δ -5.80pp) is the target; timeframe buckets within threshold and unaffected product lines are explicitly out of scope. The mix-lift component rests on an unconfirmed industry prior that premium mix improves blended margin — it is treated here as a hypothesis to validate with SKU-level margin data before quantified reliance, not as fact.
options_ranked.rationale: Price-volume-mix decomposition shows revenue realization has not kept pace with input cost on the two largest change points (Synthetic Blend -7.14pp, Conventional -6.61pp). Renewal cycles and volume incentives operate outside the price-lock constraint, making this the fastest compliant commercial lever. The critic concern that the premium-mix margin relationship is an unconfirmed correlational prior is answered by gating the mix incentive behind a SKU-level margin validation prerequisite and treating the +2-3pp mix component as contingent, not committed.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 60-120 days (mix incentive immediate; pricing phased at renewal in Q3-Q4)

arguments_for: Attacks the revenue side of the margin identity without breaching the contractual price-lock, converting renewal timing into pricing leverage on the two largest change points.
Rebate-based mix incentives are self-funding if the validated premium-versus-Value margin gap exceeds the incentive cost.
arguments_against: The mix-lift mechanism rests on an unconfirmed template prior; if input-cost inflation is masking the premium margin advantage, shifting mix recovers little.
Compliance depends entirely on renewal windows falling outside the lockout period, which has not yet been verified account by account.
key_questions: What percentage of anchor-account contract value reaches renewal within the next two quarters, verified against the price-lock clause dates?
What is the current SKU-level margin gap between premium formulations and Value tier after the recent cost inflation?

implementation_triggers: SKU-level margin validation confirms premium formulations still carry at least 4pp higher gross margin than Value tier post-inflation.
Legal review confirms at least 40% of anchor-account contract value renews outside the lockout window within two quarters.
prerequisites: Contract-by-contract renewal calendar mapped against the price-lock clause before any pricing communication (Week 1-2).
SKU-level margin validation of the premium-versus-Value gap to convert the mix hypothesis into a quantified basis.
Rebate accrual budget approved for the mix incentive program.

impact_estimate.basis: Sized against the Engine Oils line decline of -5.80pp: +2.0-3.0pp from mix shift (hypothesis pending SKU-margin validation) plus +1.2-2.1pp from 3-5% renewal pricing on Synthetic Blend and Conventional; this sizes the Engine Oils segment, not the enterprise KPI.

key_assumptions.assumption: Premium formulations retain a materially higher gross margin than Value tier despite base-oil inflation.
key_assumptions.provenance: SKU-level margin report showing premium-minus-Value margin gap of 4pp or more in the current period would confirm; the causal register lists this only as an unconfirmed correlational prior.

key_assumptions.assumption: A meaningful share of anchor-account contracts renew outside the price-lock window within two quarters.
key_assumptions.provenance: Contract renewal calendar cross-referenced with lockout clause dates; falsified if fewer than 40% of accounts renew in the horizon.

key_assumptions.assumption: Customers will accept 3-5% renewal price increases without volume attrition exceeding the margin gain.
key_assumptions.provenance: Renewal win-rate and volume retention at increased prices in the first two renewal cohorts.

flagged_side_effects: The quantified mix-lift component (2-3pp) relies on an unconfirmed premium-mix-to-margin relationship; if cost inflation is masking the premium advantage, that portion of the recovery does not materialize — hence the validation gate before rebate spend.
If renewal timing overlaps the lockout window on key accounts, the pricing component must be deferred, delaying 1.2-2.1pp of the estimate.

options_ranked.title: Value-Tier Cost Audit, SKU Rationalization and Portfolio Reweighting
options_ranked.description: Conduct an urgent cost-of-goods audit across the Value category (Δ -6.42pp) covering base oil procurement, packaging, and distribution spend; consolidate suppliers, optimize packaging formats, and shift the lowest-margin Conventional SKUs to direct-ship models. Then reweight commercial emphasis from Conventional toward Synthetic Blend. Consistency note: Synthetic Blend is itself currently degraded (20.64% vs 27.78% prior) — only marginally above Conventional (19.16%) — so Step 1 is to restore Synthetic Blend margins via the cost audit and procurement actions, and only then accelerate the mix reweighting once its margin advantage is re-established above roughly 24%. Scope: Value category and Conventional SKUs; product lines and periods within threshold are untouched.
options_ranked.rationale: The frame-questioning read is that this is a cost-side structural squeeze on the entire Value tier, not a fixable commercial variance — the portfolio's margin anchor (Synthetic Blend) fell hardest, ruling out demand or pricing-power loss as the primary story. Cost audit and SKU rationalization operate entirely on confirmed COGS components (base oil, packaging, distribution), avoiding the price-lock. The critic concern that de-emphasizing Conventional would cut units sold and, via the confirmed volume-to-revenue link, reduce net revenue is addressed directly: reweighting is gated behind margin restoration and a revenue-neutrality test rather than executed immediately.
options_ranked.time_to_value: 90-180 days for audit and rationalization; portfolio reweighting 6-12 months, gated

arguments_for: Targets the broadest change point in the data — the entire Value category at -6.42pp — rather than a single product, so gains compound across SKUs.
Packaging, distribution and procurement are all confirmed COGS components, so every dollar removed flows directly into Gross Margin %.
arguments_against: De-emphasizing Conventional reduces units sold, which by the confirmed volume-to-revenue relationship lowers net revenue even as blended margin % improves — a dollar-versus-ratio trade-off the board must accept explicitly.

The target of the mix shift (Synthetic Blend) is itself currently underperforming at 20.64%, so reweighting before its margins are restored would move volume toward a product only 1.5pp better than the one being de-emphasized.
key_questions: What is the gross-profit-dollar impact, not just margin %, of shifting 10-20% of Conventional volume to Synthetic Blend at current margins versus restored margins?
Which Conventional SKUs fall below a contribution-margin floor that justifies rationalization regardless of the mix question?

implementation_triggers: Synthetic Blend margin restored above approximately 24% (versus 20.64 current) before any active de-emphasis of Conventional volume.
Cost audit identifies at least 3% unit-cost reduction opportunity in Value-tier packaging or distribution.
prerequisites: Cost-of-goods audit of Value-tier base oil, packaging and distribution spend completed within 45 days.
Gross-profit-dollar model quantifying the revenue loss from Conventional volume reduction against the blended-margin gain, before any reweighting decision.
Restoration of Synthetic Blend margin (via cost actions in this option or the procurement option) as a hard gate before mix reweighting.

impact_estimate.basis: Sized against the Value category decline of -6.42pp: procurement consolidation, packaging optimization and SKU rationalization recover an estimated 50-70% of the cost-driven portion of the drop within the Value tier; this sizes the Value category segment, not the enterprise KPI.

key_assumptions.assumption: A majority (roughly 50-70%) of the Value-tier margin decline is cost-driven and recoverable through procurement, packaging, and distribution efficiency.
key_assumptions.provenance: Cost audit decomposition of the -6.42pp Value category decline; falsified if less than a third of the delta traces to controllable cost lines.

key_assumptions.assumption: Synthetic Blend margins can be restored sufficiently to re-establish it as the reweighting target.
key_assumptions.provenance: Synthetic Blend gross margin recovering above 24% for two consecutive periods.

key_assumptions.assumption: Distribution and packaging costs sum directly into COGS, so reductions flow straight to the margin ratio.
key_assumptions.provenance: Client-confirmed causal edges: distribution_cost and packaging_cost are account_category components of COGS, and COGS directly moves gross_margin_pct.

flagged_side_effects: Reweighting away from Conventional will reduce Conventional units sold and order counts, which per the confirmed volume-to-revenue relationship lowers net revenue in dollar terms even while blended margin % improves; this trade-off is gated behind a gross-profit-dollar neutrality test and Synthetic Blend margin restoration.
SKU rationalization may strand customers whose contracts reference discontinued formats, requiring transition provisions.

solutions.recommendation_rationale: The near-parity declines across Synthetic Blend (-7.14pp), Conventional (-6.61pp) and Compressor Oil (-5.86pp) are the fingerprint of a shared input-cost shock, and base oil cost is a client-confirmed component of COGS — the only fully confirmed causal path to Gross Margin % among the three mechanisms proposed. Hedging and supplier renegotiation act on that confirmed path, require no customer-facing change, and are structurally immune to the mid-quarter price-lock on anchor accounts, making the procurement intervention the right first move; the renewal-cycle pricing play and Value-tier rationalization then layer on once the unit-cost bridge confirms the shock's size and composition.

problem_reframe.situation: Gross Margin % for the Lubricants Business has dropped to 20.64 in the driving segment, with the enterprise blended margin falling from 34.43 to 29.94 (-4.49pp, -13.0%) year-to-date versus prior year-to-date — a net overall decline in Gross Margin %.
problem_reframe.complication: Performance is not uniform: the erosion is concentrated in Synthetic Blend Engine Oil (Δ -7.14pp), Conventional Engine Oil (Δ -6.61pp), Compressor Oil (Δ -5.86pp) and the Value category (Δ -6.42pp), while timeframe buckets outside the affected window remain within threshold. The synchronized decline across both premium-blend and conventional grades points to a shared cost-side driver (base oil, distribution) rather than product-specific commercial failure — and a contractual price-lock clause blocks mid-quarter list-price recovery on anchor accounts, removing the fastest commercial lever.
problem_reframe.question: Which combination of cost-side, contract-cycle, and portfolio interventions restores 3-5 percentage points of Gross Margin % in the affected engine-oil and Value-tier segments within 90-180 days without violating the anchor-account price-lock?
key_assumptions: The margin decline began around period 2026-006 and is driven primarily by COGS inflation, not demand collapse, since decline is synchronized across grades.
The price-lock clause applies to mid-quarter list-price changes only, not to renewal-cycle pricing, rebates, or cost-side actions.

proposed_option.title: Tiered Contract Renegotiation and Mix Incentive Program for Post-Lockout Renewal Cycles
proposed_option.description: Identify anchor accounts with Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil contracts expiring after the current price-lock window. Simultaneously, implement a margin-recovery mix incentive (rebate or volume bonus) for customers who shift purchase allocation from Value to Premium tier products within the lockout period. proposed_option.mechanism: The price-lock constraint prevents immediate list-price recovery, but contract renewal cycles and volume-based incentive structures operate outside that constraint. By front-loading mix improvement (Premium SKUs carry ~6–8pp higher margin per the premium_mix_pct relationship), you recover 2–3pp of the 7.14pp loss before renewal pricing takes effect. At renewal, use the improved mix and customer retention data to justify +3–5% price increases on Synthetic Blend and Conventional products, directly addressing the COGS/input-cost driver.

impact_estimate.basis: Mix-driven recovery (0-90 days): +2.0–3.0pp from Premium tier shift. Pricing recovery at renewal (phased into Q3–Q4): +1.2–2.1pp from 3–5% price increase on Synthetic Blend and Conventional SKUs, assuming 60–70% of anchor accounts are in or approaching renewal windows. Total addressable recovery is 3.2–5.1pp of the 7.14pp loss, with the balance attributable to structural base-oil cost inflation requiring longer-term sourcing or formulation strategy.

proposed_option.description: Establish a 60–90-day procurement review of base oil supply contracts for Synthetic Blend and Conventional Engine Oil lines, with explicit focus on (1) forward-curve hedging of WTI-linked base oil indices, and (2) supplier margin renegotiation to recover 40–60% of the observed cost shock through volume commitments or longer-term fixed-price tranches. proposed_option.mechanism: Base oil cost is a direct component of COGS (confirmed causal link). A 7.14 pp margin decline on Synthetic Blend implies base oil cost per unit has risen materially relative to net revenue. Hedging forward exposure and renegotiating supplier terms will either lock in lower future costs (hedging) or redistribute the cost burden via volume/commitment leverage (renegotiation), directly reducing the COGS numerator and restoring gross margin % without requiring list-price changes on locked accounts.

impact_estimate.basis: Base oil typically represents 35–50% of COGS in synthetic blend formulations. A 7.14 pp margin decline implies ~10–15% cost inflation on base oil input. Hedging 60–70% of forward volume and renegotiating 30–40% of current supplier cost can recover 50–75% of the observed shock, translating to 3.5–5.2 pp margin recovery on Synthetic Blend, with spillover gains on Conventional (+2.5–3.8 pp) via shared procurement leverage.
